keep: Retire from the shop as early as you can afford to — then spend the second half inventing institutions.
lede: A printer who retired at forty-two and spent the second half of his life inventing a country's institutions — the patron saint of every small press, this one included.
copy: The runaway apprentice from Boston built Philadelphia's best print shop, made Poor Richard's Almanack a franchise, and retired from active business at forty-two — the pivot the whole life turns on. What followed: the experiments that made lightning electricity and won him the Copley Medal; the stove, the lightning rod and bifocals, none patented, on the stated principle that we should serve others freely with our inventions as we enjoy theirs.

His deeper trade was institutions. A subscription library, a fire company, a hospital, an academy that became a university, a learned society, a postal system — Franklin repeatedly noticed a missing piece of civic machinery and simply organised it, using the same club of tradesmen, the Junto, as his laboratory. Then the largest institution of all: he is the only man who signed the Declaration of Independence, the treaty with France he charmed into existence, the peace with Britain, and the Constitution.

The Autobiography gave the world its first great self-improvement programme — thirteen virtues, a weekly tracking chart, and the dry admission that he never mastered humility but learned to fake it profitably. Read it as he wrote it: a curated performance by history's shrewdest personal brand, wise about exactly how such performances work.

bio.why: The most readable full life, strongest on the printer and the diplomat. H.W. Brands's 'The First American' (2000) is the fuller scholarly alternative if you want one degree more depth.

contested: Isaacson writes to his house template — the ingenious, pragmatic outsider — and historians find him lighter on Franklin's decades as a slaveholder who turned abolitionist only late. The Autobiography, the foundation of the legend, is self-presentation by a master of it; treat it as an artifact to interpret, not a record to trust.
